# Lab Notebook {#sec-lab}

This is the original session, retold as a sequence of probes. The point of
the retelling is the order. A hypothesis was written down. The next call
confirmed it, qualified it, or killed it. That rhythm is worth more than
any particular flag.

The script is a private scratch file. What follows is the part that
generalizes. Where a printed `REF` count depended on RStudio holding extra
references, the count is reported as a phenomenon, not as a constant.

## Where `inspect` comes from

The file opens on the right question: is `inspect` itself a SEXP you can
study, or a door into the C runtime? It is a door. `.Internal(inspect(x))`
calls `do_inspect`. The value you pass is the SEXP. The printer is an
entry in the internals table. @sec-header decodes a line. The rest of
this notebook assumes that decoding.

A classed list (`structure(list(x = 1L), class = "obj")`) showed the whole
vocabulary at once: a `VECSXP` with `OBJ` and `ATT`, a child `INTSXP`, and
an attribute `LISTSXP` whose tags were the symbols `names` and `class`.
Those symbols were locked, saturated, and old (`g1`). The character data
was a cached `CHARSXP`. One object, three worlds: generic vector, atomic
vector, cons chain.

## Nil, and the hypothesis that overreached

`NULL`, `c()`, and `pairlist()` shared an address, type 0, `REF(65535)`.
`identical()` stayed true under the strict switches, including
`extptr.as.ref = TRUE`. The comment drew the natural conclusion: any
genuinely empty thing is that cell.

`list()` and `alist()` retired the conclusion for generic vectors. Each
was a fresh length-zero `VECSXP`. `integer()`, `double()`, `character()`,
`logical()`, `complex()`, and `raw()` retired it for the atomics. The
comment had guessed that lists were `VECSXP` *because they need method
dispatch*. The type is older than that need. Dispatch consults the class
and the `OBJ` bit. An empty list with no class is already not Nil.
@sec-empties is the write-up. The primitive-generic vectors printed next
to the hypothesis (`.S3PrimitiveGenerics`, `.internalGenerics`) are about
which verbs are wired into C, not about why the empty list exists.

`typeof(character())` is `"character"` and the SEXP type is `STRSXP`. The
comment's `STRSEXP` was a reasonable coinage. The cache of individual
strings is the `CHARSXP` layer underneath.

## Primitives

`sum` and `+` and `c` printed as builtins, type 8, saturated, old.
`[` printed as a special, type 7. Printing a primitive shows
`.Primitive("sum")` rather than a body. That is the applicative-versus-raw
split from @sec-in-context, met in the wild. These types are not mythical.
They are what `typeof` of the function returns, any time you ask.

## A double wearing a class

`bit64::integer64()` has `typeof` `"double"` and inspects as a `REALSXP`
with `OBJ`, `ATT`, and class `"integer64"`. The comment called this
interesting and then, later, connected it to factors. Factors felt like
they might be "more of an object" in the `OBJSXP` sense. They are not.
`is.object(factor(1))` is true because the `OBJ` bit is set. `typeof` is
`"integer"`. The historical SEXP types for factors were 11 and 12, and
they were withdrawn. The "lie about storage" pattern is the living design.
@sec-in-context keeps the two meanings of "object" apart so they can stay
apart.

## Conditions, left open on purpose

The long comment is the seed of @sec-signals. Conditions look like a
CLOS-style system, the surrounding culture uses them as exceptions, and
errors-as-values (purrr, rlang results, validators) sit nearby unused. The
comment's own correction is the one to keep: it is S3 on a signaling
foundation, not CLOS. The resemblance to Pitman is in the *shape* ---
signal, handle on the live stack, restart --- not in the implementation.
The frustration with catching an error only to throw another one is a
layering point, not a reason to abandon signals.

## S7 classes are closures

`S7::class_any` inspected as a length-zero `VECSXP` with class `S7_any`.
Not a class constructor. `S7::new_class("myclass")` inspected as a
`CLOSXP` with attributes for the class metadata, a body that calls
`S7::new_object`, and a parent whose body was already a `BCODESXP` inside
the S7 namespace. `typeof` of the class object is `"closure"`.

That dump is also where byte code, language objects, and the Nil formal
list show up without anyone asking for them. A compiled package function
contains a `BCODESXP`. A call in the body is a `LANGSXP`. An empty formal
list is Nil. "Types you never see" are types you see the moment the value
you asked about is implemented with them.

## R6 generators are environments

`typeof(R6::R6Class())` is `"environment"`. The inspect paste is long
because the generator is an environment full of closures, and the clone
method's body is a program that allocates more environments, remaps
function enclosures, locks them, and registers a finalizer for
`$finalize`. The symbol `<<-` appears inside that generated code. So does
`.__enclos_env__`. The class attribute on the generator is
`R6ClassGenerator`.

This is the Scheme object, written out by a code generator. It is also a
practical demonstration that `<<-` is not foreign to serious R. R6 uses
superassignment *inside a known enclosure*, the object environment it just
built. That is the declared version. The fragile version is the one where
the enclosure is whatever happened to call you. Seeing both in the same
afternoon is how the distinction becomes obvious.

## Weak references

`rlang::new_weakref(new.env(parent = emptyenv()), value = "x")` has
`typeof` `"weakref"` and inspects as type 23, `WEAKREFSXP`. The comment
asked whether this is only an rlang convention. The type is a runtime
type. The comfortable constructor is a package. `reg.finalizer` is what
base gives you for the adjacent problem. @sec-in-context puts external
pointers next to weak references so the two stop sharing a single vague
reputation.

The same stretch of the file quotes the internals manual on a fossil:
"user databases," apparently the old Omegahat `RObjectTables` package, an
undocumented lookup hook. It is a good reminder that the manual still
contains archaeology. Read it next to the source when a sentence seems
to describe a feature you have never seen. Sometimes the feature is real
and hidden. Sometimes it is a scar.

## The question the dumps were heading toward

The file then states the design question cleanly. Reference semantics
make in-place change observable, which is what you want for invalidation,
caches, and anything reactive. Values plus replacement functions can
imitate some of that, at the cost of a new object. Low-level facts do not
design a package by themselves. They tell you which promises the package
is allowed to make. The rest of the file is an S7 experiment that takes
the promise seriously.

## An S7 assignment changes the address

`s_x` was defined with a single `class_any` property. The class object was
a `CLOSXP`. An instance was created. `lobstr::obj_addr` was recorded.
`my_x@p <- "aaa"` was evaluated. The address changed. The new node was an
`OBJSXP` with `OBJ` and `ATT`, class `c("s_x", "S7_object")`, a pointer
back at the class, and a property record whose visible names included
`name`, `class`, `getter`, `setter`, and `validator`.

That is the value illusion, holding, for a class system that people
sometimes describe as "more OO" and therefore somehow reference-like. The
replacement syntax looks like mutation. The address says a new value was
born. R6 would have kept the address. The two dumps together are the
fork in @sec-illusion and @sec-containers, obtained before any of those
chapters were written.

The property record is the other souvenir. The slots for a strict
property were present and, in this definition, empty. @sec-types hangs
the authoring argument on that observation. The docs can show `class_any`.
The node still has a place to put a validator. The next person who defines
`p` gets to decide whether the place stays empty.

## What to rerun

When a R release moves, the probes worth repeating are the ones the
verification script already pins, plus three that need a human eye:

- `inspect(1:1e9)` and see whether you are looking at an ALTREP node
  rather than a billion integers
- `lobstr::ref` before and after `x[1] <-` on a shared vector, and watch
  the count force a copy
- a `withCallingHandlers` / `withRestarts` pair small enough to feel the
  stack stay alive, next to a `tryCatch` that unwinds it

The script in `verification/` guards the claims that should not drift:
Nil's identity with `c()` and `pairlist()`, the independence of `list()`,
the types of the typed empties, the factor representation, and builtin
versus special. If one of those fails, the book is describing a different
R than the one you have, and the book loses.
